# Game manufacturing route selection — concept pack (small)

> Source-anchored research for Game manufacturing route selection. Run status: COMPLETED.

<!-- generated by llms-concept-abstractor v1.4.1 · generated 2026-11-06 · budgeted to ≈8000 tokens; the full catalogue is llms-full.txt -->

## Structure and components

- [statement] Panda describes two distinct approval samples: a near-final Pre-Production Copy of printed components before mass production, and a full Mass Production Copy before final assembly. This documents a supplier review process, not independently measured production quality or a guaranteed defect rate. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06) — https://pandagm.com/our-process/
- [statement] Panda describes approval of the pre-production copy and component samples as the gate before mass production starts. This documents a contract-manufacturing approval step, not independent proof that production output will meet the buyer’s quality requirements. (low confidence) — https://pandagm.com/our-process/

## How it works

- [statement] Smartpress treats collating as grouping pieces into a specific sequence, but says collated sets ship unseparated unless a bundling option is selected, and belly bands are not automatic. Methodological implication: specify complete sets and physical set separation when comparing a trade-print route with an assembled-game service. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06) — https://smartpress.com/support/product-faq/collated-printing-faq

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] An automatic-duplex feature alone does not qualify an owned printer for thick card stock: Epson’s ET-8550 support page says automatic double-sided printing is unsupported on glossy, thick and certain matte papers. This limitation is model-specific, not a claim that every owned printer has the same restriction. (low confidence) — https://epson.com/faq/SPT_C11CJ21201~faq-00004fb-et8500_8550?faq_cat=faq-8796127602764
- [statement] Epson documents quality and handling qualifications for an owned printer: its scuff-reduction setting can reduce quality or slow printing, and manual duplex printing requires the ink to dry completely before the sheet is reloaded. Treat these as workflow constraints to verify on the intended stock, not measured production rates. (low confidence) — https://download4.epson.biz/sec_pubs/et-8550_series/useg/en/GUID-85133602-1F39-4AF0-9CAB-A0DC7C3C11A1.htm

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] Smartpress advises against Soft Touch laminate for playing cards because its tactile surface can make shuffling harder. This is supplier advice rather than independent shuffle testing; a premium-sounding finish should not be assumed to improve game handling. (low confidence) — https://smartpress.com/support/product-faq/collated-printing-faq
- [statement] Methodological inference: compare routes against a common physical specification and proof, rather than just a shared deck label. PrintNinja separates card stock, finish and packaging choices; Graphic Lab recommends a proof on its actual material, while Smartpress warns that a particular laminate can impair shuffling. (medium confidence) — https://printninja.com/printing-products/card-game-printing/ · keywords: Game manufacturing route selection · also: https://www.graphiclabinc.com/custom-board-game-printing, https://smartpress.com/support/product-faq/collated-printing-faq
- [statement] Qualify local trade printing with a finished card sample rather than sheet-print capability alone (inference from historical operator evidence). Cole’s guide treats shuffleable cards as specialist production and recommends samples. In Koster’s 2013 comparison, his POD deck shuffled better than a copy-shop punch-out version, but had registration issues; the punch-out cards had rough perforated edges. These dated accounts do not establish current supplier performance. (medium confidence) — https://www.starfleetgames.com/fc/book/4-game_production-2.pdf · keywords: Game manufacturing route selection · also: https://www.raphkoster.com/2013/09/05/a-little-card-game-prototype/

## Facts and statements

- [statement] The Game Crafter advertises no minimum order for a designed game and allows purchase of a single copy. This establishes a supplier-stated POD entry option; it does not establish suitability of an unspecified card construction. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06) — https://www.thegamecrafter.com/
- [statement] Bulk entry requirements depend on the supplier: PrintNinja states a minimum of 500 decks for its offset card-game service; Panda states a minimum of 1,500 games. These are supplier order minima, not economic break-even thresholds. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06) — https://printninja.com/printing-products/card-game-printing/ · keywords: Game manufacturing route selection · also: https://pandagm.com/our-process/
- [statement] Graphic Lab advertises one-off custom playing-card prototypes and recommends an actual proof on its material. Its page describes glossy or matte vinyl and lamination; methodological implication: verify paper-card construction before treating this local-shop offering as equivalent to a paper deck. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06) — https://www.graphiclabinc.com/custom-board-game-printing
- [statement] For an owned ET-8550 route, Epson instructs users to let ink dry completely before manually printing the reverse side, warns that dark or heavily saturated images can smudge the reverse, and notes that its thick-paper setting reduces print speed. These are manufacturer operating constraints, not measured finished-deck throughput. (low confidence) — https://epson.com/faq/SPT_C11CJ21201~faq-00007f6-et8500_8550?faq_cat=faq-8796127537228
- [statement] Epson identifies nozzle checks, head cleaning, head alignment and paper-path cleaning among remedies for ET-8550 smeared output, and warns that Power Cleaning consumes substantial ink. An owned-printing route therefore needs a maintenance allowance; this source does not quantify its frequency or cost per game. (low confidence) — https://epson.com/faq/SPT_C11CJ21201~faq-00007f6-et8500_8550?faq_cat=faq-8796127537228
- [statement] The Game Crafter defines drift as print-to-cut misalignment and warns that borders make drift more apparent. Its advice to include bleed and follow template border guidance limits the assumption that outsourcing automatically produces perfectly centered card borders. (low confidence) — https://help.thegamecrafter.com/article/392-drift
- [statement] Ars Technica reported a Cards Against Humanity spokesperson’s account of an earlier US-factory trial as more expensive, slower and lower quality, with games rejected for production errors. This is an attributed experience involving that supplier trial, not independently audited evidence about all US printers or this commissioned game. (low confidence) (verified as of 2025-10-11) — https://arstechnica.com/culture/2025/10/why-doesnt-cards-against-humanity-print-its-game-in-the-us-its-complicated/
- [statement] Published order floors distinguish specific route candidates: The Game Crafter permits a single copy, PrintNinja advertises a minimum of 500 decks and uses offset printing, and Panda advertises a minimum of 1,500 games. These are supplier-specific entry conditions, not a universal volume threshold for choosing a route. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06) — https://www.thegamecrafter.com/ · keywords: Game manufacturing route selection · also: https://printninja.com/printing-products/card-game-printing/, https://pandagm.com/our-process/
- [statement] For an ownership candidate, Epson documents that the ET-8550 rear paper feed slot accepts thick paper up to 1.3 mm. This is a media-path specification; it does not establish compatibility with the commissioned game stock, shuffle feel, or finished-deck output. (low confidence) — https://download4.epson.biz/sec_pubs/et-8550_series/useg/en/GUID-311A8905-0C48-4D76-8545-E44BAB44DB88.htm
- [statement] Looney Labs’ FAQ records historical use of a nearby printer for black-and-white art cards. This is an operator example of a local printing route for that limited product; it does not establish that an arbitrary local shop can supply a finished paper party-game deck. (low confidence) — https://faq.looneylabs.com/non-gameplay-questions/game-design-publishing
- [statement] In an October 2025 account reported by Ars Technica, Cards Against Humanity described a previous US factory trial as more expensive, slower and lower quality than its existing production. Ars also explicitly says US card-game production is possible. This is an attributed single-company experience, not evidence that domestic manufacture is impossible or necessarily inferior for this project. (low confidence) — https://arstechnica.com/culture/2025/10/why-doesnt-cards-against-humanity-print-its-game-in-the-us-its-complicated/
